posts.content:
I’m in the mood to break some manufacturing myths today. 🛠️

There is one rule people treat as absolute law: start with 3D printing, and once your volume gets high enough, switch to injection molding because it’s cheaper per unit.
It makes perfect sense on a spreadsheet. But on the factory floor, the math is completely different.

At Prusa, we run one of the largest 24/7 3D print farms in the world right alongside our own injection molding lines. We see the real data every single day.
Take the display case on our printers, for example. The 3D-printed part cost us around €0.25. The injection-molded version costs €0.18, and the mold itself was roughly €6,000. If you look at the graph, it takes about 80,000 units to break even and recoup those tooling costs.
But unit cost is not the end of the story. We didn't make the switch just to save seven cents.

The display case is large, and printing tens of thousands of them was taking up a massive amount of time. Moving it to injection molding cleared a bottleneck.
This is the power of a true hybrid approach.

By moving mature, high-volume parts to molding, we instantly freed up our print farm. Now, those printers can do what they do best: produce parts that actually NEED to be printed, things that change often or require fast iteration. You don't have to choose just one technology; you use both to balance the factory.

In fact, we lean into this hybrid model so much that we have other parts in our factory where we chose injection molding even though the unit cost actually went up.
It sounds crazy, I know. We are currently putting together a deep dive with all our internal data on exactly why we did this, so keep an eye out for it soon! 👀
Until then, I want to hear your experience. Molding, printing, or a hybrid of both? And why? What metric do you apply? 👇

#Manufacturing #3DPrinting #InjectionMolding #Engineering #Prusa #HybridManufacturing

posts.content:
If we are serious about bringing manufacturing back to the West 🏭, we have to rethink how things are made. One of the most practical ways to do that is by adopting true multi-material 3D printing.

And please, do not confuse this with multi-color printing, that's for toys and statues. I'm talking about combining a rigid engineering polymer (like Carbon-Filled Nylon) with a soft, flexible rubber (like TPU) in a single run.

Trying to push these different polymers through one nozzle is an engineering nightmare. The temperatures clash, and the process is slow and wasteful. To do this reliably, you need a Toolchanger, a system in which every material gets its own perfectly tuned hotend.

When you have that capability sitting on a desktop, it completely changes how you design products:

💧 Water-Soluble Supports: Intricate parts need supports you usually have to break away with pliers. Now, you can print the main part in a tough polymer and the supports in PVA. Drop the part in water, the supports dissolve completely, and you get a flawless surface. 

⚙️ Zero-Assembly Mechanics: Print a rigid enclosure with a tough, flexible TPU hinge already built in. It comes off the bed ready to use: no gluing, no screws, no assembly line. 

💰 Smart Material Use: Need incredible strength? Print just the outer shell in an expensive carbon-filled nylon, and fill the inside with an affordable basic filament.
When you can securely produce complex, multi-property end-use parts right in your own workshop, you stop relying on fragile overseas supply chains. You keep your IP in-house.

The materials are ready. The hardware has finally caught up.
If you could combine two completely different materials into one single part today, what would you build? Let me know below. 👇

posts.content:
How do you save 600,000 USD and years of cumulative supply wait time? 
You stop waiting for a global supply chain to ship you a spare part, and you manufacture it yourself right where it is needed.

The U.S. Marine Corps recently published an incredibly interesting use case about a communications antenna mast that kept breaking from wear and tear in the field. Under the traditional supply chain, replacing this single part meant ordering a massive assembly. It cost $5,644.37 and took over seven months to arrive. If a critical piece of hardware sits idle for 220 days waiting on a shipping container, your operational readiness drops to zero.

So, an engineer on the ground decided to fix it. With 3D printing.

There is a great technical lesson in the text about how he did it. When he first 3D printed the replacement vertically, it kept snapping under stress. In printing, layer orientation dictates your structural strength. By switching the print orientation to horizontal, he aligned the continuous filament lines with the load forces. The part passed a month of brutal field exercises.

Look at how the math changes when you move production directly to the point of need:
- Traditional cost: $5,644.37 per unit
- Traditional wait time: 220+ days
- On-demand material cost: ~$10.00
- On-demand print time: 10 hours

Total impact: 107 parts printed, saving $600,000 and cutting out 60 years of cumulative wait time.

The official military article doesn't explicitly name the hardware brand they used at their Innovation Campus. But if you look closely at the photos, those are our Prusa CORE One printers running in the background.

If we are serious about bringing manufacturing back to the West, we have to treat 3D printers as serious industrial tools. When handling proprietary designs, you need reliable, secure hardware that keeps your data and fixes strictly within your facility.

What about your own operations? What is a part you now regularly print on-demand instead of waiting weeks for a supplier to ship it? Let me know below. 👇

posts.content:
Yesterday, I mentioned how Canadian engineers are using 3D printing to literally change the world. Here is exactly what I meant.

When it comes to medical hardware and prosthetics, traditional manufacturing can be incredibly slow and restrictive. Upper-limb prosthetics can cost thousands of dollars and take months to arrive. For a patient, waiting that long isn't just a huge inconvenience: it can lead to muscle atrophy and a painful delay in regaining everyday skills.
The team at the Victoria Hand Project (at the University of Victoria) realized that manufacturing these devices centrally and shipping them across the world was the wrong approach. So, they built an incredibly clever solution.

Instead of shipping hands, they ship a "technology transfer" model. They are building a truly worldwide, decentralized network. From Guatemala and Haiti to rural clinics in Kenya, Nepal, and Ukraine, they equip partner facilities across 11 countries with the 3D printing hardware, materials, and a highly automated Autodesk Fusion 360 workflow. Any trained clinician anywhere in the world can scan a patient's limb, and the software automatically generates a perfect-fitting socket, completely removing the engineering bottleneck.

This decentralized system is making a massive impact right now at the Arol Plus clinic in Lviv, where they are treating civilians and soldiers with traumatic limb loss. By printing the prosthetics right on-site, patients receive functional limbs in days instead of weeks. And the material cost drops to a fraction of traditional methods, around just $150 USD per hand.

To keep up with the constant demand, the Arol Plus clinic runs a fleet of Original Prusa XLs 24/7. In a war zone, grid stability is a serious issue. But thanks to the Power Panic function, if the clinic loses electricity, the printers simply save their position and resume exactly where they left off when the power returns. No wasted plastic, no lost time.

This is exactly what I mean when I talk about the endgame of reshoring. It’s not just about business or supply chains. It’s about having the power to produce life-changing hardware exactly where and when it is needed. And just as importantly, it’s about having the minds and the passion to actually engineer these kinds of solutions in the first place.

Huge respect to Dr. Nick Dechev, the VHP team in Canada, and the clinicians on the ground in Ukraine. 🇨🇦🇺🇦

What other industries do you think could benefit the most from a shift to decentralized, local manufacturing? Let me know below! 👇

‼️ PRUSA × INDX for CORE One is here.

With this release, desktop 3D printing enters its endgame - not the end of progress, but the endgame of compromises.

Eight independent toolheads. Eight loaded materials. Different nozzle sizes ready at all times. No unload/load dance. No wipe tower. Almost no waste.

A true multi-material toolchanger for the desktop.

✅ 8 independent tools. 8 loaded materials. Different nozzle sizes ready at all times

✅ A true 8-nozzle toolchanger - not a filament switcher

✅ Abrasion-resistant hardened nozzles (INDX)

✅ True high flow with CHT geometry - fast printing with validated materials (INDX)

✅ Low-latency temperature control with induction heating and low-mass nozzles. Fast heat-up, fast cool-down, and almost no ooze from parked tools (INDX)

✅ Large-diameter dynamic dual-drive gears. Grip strength self-adjusts based on the loaded material during pickup (INDX)

✅ Accelerometer

✅ Class-leading loadcell mesh calibration

✅ Fast eddy-current toolhead offset calibration with ambient-noise cancellation (PRUSA)

✅ Priming outside the print area, with real print back-pressure simulation. Only 13 mg / 0.013 g of material to fully prime - up to 10× less than competing systems (PRUSA)

✅ Waste/priming pellets are formed for direct recycling. No grinding or pre-processing needed before going back into a filament extruder (PRUSA)

✅ No waste/prime tower - the tool is fully pre-primed before printing (PRUSA)

✅ True tool-change time: 10-17 seconds per change, depending on material. That’s from the last extrusion of one material to the first extrusion of the next, directly on the model itself (PRUSA)

✅ Enclosed heated chamber and automatic top vent for low-temperature materials

What a time to be alive. Having this at home, in the office, or in the lab would have been hard to believe five years ago.

Huge shoutout to Bondtech AB for INDX, and to my team for the rest of the innovations needed to make this awesome package possible ❤️

posts.content:
Watching the Artemis mission succeed was incredible. We are officially going back to the Moon! But now that we've proven we can fly there, we have to tackle the next challenge: actually bringing stuff with us.
Launching mass into orbit is still ridiculously expensive. If we want a permanent presence up there, the traditional supply chain is a massive bottleneck. You can't exactly rely on next-day delivery when the shipping address is a lunar crater... We can't keep sending every single tool and replacement part from Earth. Printing parts FOR space is just the beginning; printing them IN space is the endgame.
But to get to that endgame, we first have to master the materials. Because whether a part is printed on a desk here on Earth or eventually inside a lunar base, it has to survive a vacuum. And the biggest threat to plastics up there isn't just the temperature swings, it’s outgassing.  Standard plastics release trapped gases that condense on and completely destroy sensitive optics and sensors.

We partnered with the aerospace systems engineers at TRL Space to fix this.
Here is what we built with Prusament PC Space Grade Black:
👉🏻 Perfect Purity: It achieved a perfect 0.00% Collected Volatile Condensable Material (CVCM) in ESA-standard tests. This means zero volatile material is released to contaminate mission instruments.
 👉🏻 Hardware Protection: It’s electrostatically dissipative (ESD safe). It safely discharges static buildup instead of frying onboard electronics.
But here is the best part: you don't need a proprietary, million-dollar industrial machine to use it. You can print flight-ready parts right on a desktop printer, without even needing an enclosure.
This makes space technology development accessible to a much broader group of researchers and companies. We don't just want to launch tools to lunar bases and orbital stations, we want to print them when we get there. Soon, I hope!

I’m genuinely curious to see what the community and the industry will actually build with this. And it got me thinking: what other specialized materials or specific properties are you currently missing in your workflow? Let me know. 👇

I had a great discussion at the Formnext - Where ideas take shape roundtable on the “democratisation” of Additive Manufacturing. 

My key message was simple: democratisation isn’t just about low prices - it’s about data control, supplier diversity, and keeping our ability to manufacture locally. With more than 90% of the desktop 3D printer market now produced in China, that diversity is disappearing fast.

I also reminded the audience that Prusa Research is the last European/US 3D printer manufacturer still standing - producing machines at scale. And why does it matter? The same desktop printer that makes toys can also make prototypes and parts for companies such as NASA, SpaceX or Volkswagen. 3D printing has become strategic industry.

Few key snippets from my co-panelists.
Jan Lukas Waibel mentioned how understanding grows once customers see real AM results. Christian Seidel rightfully pointed out the need for standards, quality rules, and clarity about limitations. And Stefanie Brickwede highlighted the importance of secure, trusted suppliers for critical infrastructure.

I couldn’t agree more:
➡️ We must open competition, not let it collapse into a single state-backed monopoly.
➡️ We need secure, audited, trusted printers for sensitive environments.
➡️ And we must keep 3D printing affordable and accessible, because democratisation without security is not democratisation at all.

Glad to see this debate happening at Formnext - and I hope more will follow.

Our game. But their rules?

Last week in New York, not even a historic blizzard was going to keep me off the stage at Additive Manufacturing Strategies. The stakes were too high to stay home.

I went to NYC to talk about a critical shift in our industry: The 3D printing market as we knew it is gone. China decided to take it. And they are doing it by any means, with no rules.

Here is the reality the industry is facing:

👉🏻 State-Sponsored Takeover: 3D printing companies are competing against aggressive tax subsidies, direct grants, and massive unfair practices.

👉🏻 The Patent Flood: 3D printing community innovations are being met with deliberate patent trolling and the exploitation of an outdated IP system.

👉🏻 Data Security Threats: With China's recent intelligence and data security laws, guarantees like "data is encrypted" or "stored in the EU" are completely meaningless. Should I post the tldr how it works? 

I didn’t show up just to play the 'wise man' and tell everyone that we’re screwed. I went to share a plan on how to fight it.

At Prusa, we aren’t waiting for permission to fight back. We are already making specialized hardware for critical infrastructure, like the CORE One L, driving U.S. reshoring directly from our facility in Delaware, and much more. But more on that later.

The market and the rules are changing. Innovations and manufacturing will be made by someone. Let's make sure it's us.

If you and your company feel the same way, or if you are tired of competing in a rigged game, send me a message. I have an idea you might be interested in ...

PS: If you want the full deep-dive, including an opening keynote by my good friend Joris Peels, I put a link to the complete summary of the New York event in the comments below. 👇

posts.content:
I feel like a lot of people still look at 3D printing and think it’s just for enthusiasts making Star Wars figures in their bedrooms.
But it’s far more than that, and is in fact a crucial part of how modern industries work. And truthfully, that’s partly our fault as manufacturers for not educating the public enough.
If you go on Reddit or Facebook, you see the hobbyist side because makers love to share what they build. But you rarely see the industrial side. Many companies treat their 3D printing operations as a massive competitive advantage, keeping their R&D under the wraps. But when the curtain does pull back...

Here is what is actually happening on the ground:

Automotive: At Škoda Auto, rapid mass production of 3D-printed parts during COVID-19 supply chain problems prevented delays to over 13,000 vehicles. They also modified their production machinery using printed parts, reducing wear and saving thousands of dollars each month.

Aerospace: Shark Aero Ltd manufactures the fastest ultralight aircraft in the world using over 100 3D-printed components. By printing functional cockpit and engine parts, they save ~100 work hours per plane.

Particle Physics: Even CERN relies on 3D printing. They print prototypes, custom tools, and the tiny beads that carry optical wires during the calibration of the Large Hadron Collider's 27km tunnel. Printed parts keep the largest machine in the world aligned. Without creating accidental black holes…

We want to talk about this reality publicaly, show you what is actually possible, and, most importantly, inspire the next generation of engineers.

There is a reason our machines are used by NASA, SpaceX, ESA, and CERN. When you are operating at that level, it comes down to trust, reliability, and security. With the rapid advances made in recent years, 3D printers are no longer just simple machines. With network connectivity, onboard cameras, and complex firmware, they are fully functioning industrial computers. That level of connectivity brings incredible advantages, but it also comes with a serious warning attachedl: connected devices send data. If you are printing your company's most sensitive, unreleased IP, you need to know exactly where that data is going. Providing that absolute certainty, and keeping your innovation strictly in your own hands, is exactly why Siemens recently chose us as a preferred supplier.

Do you have an interesting 3D-printing project you and your company would like to share? Tell us in the comments or send a DM, and we’ll contact you to help tell your story! 👇

Virtually no waste? That was the real endgame. 🤔
 #PRUSAxINDX

For years, multi-material desktop 3D printing had one unavoidable tax: purge waste.

Unload, load, wipe, build a tower, throw material away, repeat.

With PRUSA × INDX for CORE One, we are finally attacking that problem at the source.

🐜 Only 13 milligrams / 0.013 g of material per tool change - about 1/5 of the previous best-in-class purge amount.

♻️ The waste is formed as a tiny pellet designed for direct recycling. No grinding or pre-processing needed before it goes back into a filament extruder.

💉 The nozzle is fully primed outside the print area, against the same back-pressure as during real printing. That means no prime tower, no compromise on print quality.

💡 Fun engineering detail: the pellet is formed in one cycle, but ejected from the mold in the next one, after it has fully cooled down.

INDX and the new priming/wiping system were the unlocks.

This feels like the final cherry on top of our 10-year quest to solve the waste problem in multi-material desktop 3D printing.

Since I posted my “Open hardware desktop 3D printing is dead - you just don't know it yet” article, you’ve been asking me about “that patent” 🤔 I didn’t want you to miss the forest (thousands of filings since 2020) just because of one tree. But let’s take a look now. In this case: the MMU multiplexer (we open sourced it 9 years ago). Anycubic (another IDG Capital-backed company) used the tactic of filing in China for an easy initial grant: CN 222407171 U ➡️ DE 20 2024 100 001 U1 ➡️ US 2025/0144881 A1. The playbook: file a Chinese utility model (10-year patent, same protections, lower examination, already granted) ➡️ claim that priority in Germany (again as a utility model, already granted) ➡️ file in the US. Cheap to file, but expensive and time-consuming to fight. I already wrote why prior art isn’t a magic wand that solves it immediately in my article ⤵️ 

This is state encouraged practice across the whole 3DP industry, what is your protocol to protect your new IP when using your 3D printer❓

posts.content:
🚨 THE 6 BEST THINGS ABOUT THE NEW PRUSA CORE ONE L

1️⃣ Fits on a table, print volume ~ 30 liters / 1 cubic foot, runs on standard power!

The print volume is 300×300×330 mm – plenty of space for large, durable models in a single piece. The chamber goes to 60°C, creating the perfect environment for many advanced materials.

2️⃣ AC convection heatbed with <2°C variance across 99% of the surface.

Nothing can beat a solid chunk of aluminum. Plus, we have dual-loop heating, beautifully uniform heat distribution with a variance of less than 2% across 99% of its surface, killing warping and cold corners. Two fans on the heatbed’s underside (paired with two air deflectors) are designed to warm up the chamber quickly.

3️⃣ 60°C heated chamber with smart temperature management and exhaust port for HVAC or filtration.

A true “start and forget” machine. The CORE One already did a lot to automate the chamber temperature, but this goes one step further with the automated top vent opening and closing. Plus, the new heat distribution system warms up the chamber much faster.

4️⃣ Quality high-speed printing with YOUR materials, not just ours.

A genuine Bondtech 🇸🇪 CHT nozzle comes pre-mounted. It’s engineered for high flow with all filaments because speed means nothing if you can’t use the materials you’ve already tested and qualified for production. Special internal geometry melts filament faster through optimized heat transfer. A wear-resistant nozzle for abrasive materials is included with every printer.

5️⃣ Unpack and print! Precalibrated from the factory.

The CORE One L is available as an assembled printer only. It comes fully pre-calibrated from the factory, including Phase Stepping and Input Shaper (more on these later). When you unpack it, you simply select the preferred language and complete an optional connection wizard. It’s a complete package with a 1080p camera, two nozzles, a comprehensive Prusa Academy course, and more.

6️⃣ Security ready for critical infrastructure.

Our printers were always focused on security – embedded platform, open-source firmware, removable radios and cameras, encrypted flash drive as an addon, and offline-first design. We feel that security matters now more than ever, so we’re bringing new security options.

Let's build something great 💪

During my recent trip to Australia, I had the pleasure of meeting many printer operators who have been using their Original Prusa MK3s 3D printers since the product's launch nearly 7 years ago. What's truly remarkable is that these users have no plans to retire their machines anytime soon! 🤯 It's a testament to our philosophy of prioritizing function over form, which ultimately creates the most value for our customers in the long run.
Several factors contribute to the MK3s' impressive longevity:

1️⃣ Repairability - The printer is designed with easy repairs in mind. It's hard to imagine a failure mode that would make you say, "Oh, this isn't worth fixing. I'll just throw it away and buy a new one!" The design practically invites repairs, even if it doesn't win any beauty contests. 😇

2️⃣ Continuous Improvements - The MK3s gets significantly better over time through firmware and slicer updates. In 2023 alone, we've already released 7 major firmware updates! 🤯

3️⃣ Upgradeability - We offer hardware upgrades to keep the machine up-to-date, reducing the incentive to purchase a brand-new printer.

I believe there's a very good chance that tens of thousands of MK3s will still be running strong for 10+ years, truly living up to the WORKHORSE label. 🧡 And with the same design principles, the XL and MK4 will undoubtedly serve you well into the 2030s. 💪

Now, I'd love to hear your stories! How long have you been running your MK3s? Are you planning to upgrade to the MK3.5? Let me know in the comments below!

posts.content:
Story time! 📖 Let's talk about the history behind the now legendary Prusa3D t-shirt design - Everyone is a maker, only I am a printer PRUSA

I have already been working on the RepRap 💚 3D printers for some time (RepRap is an open-source 3D printer project), Prusa Mendel (https://lnkd.in/eJtfu8n3) was still the latest and greatest, but most of my interactions with the community were just via IRC chat (something like Discord, but simpler and better 😅). In the early days, we didn't get to meet much in real life. (This later changed when my design got simple enough we could throw a build class over the weekend with a group of enthusiasts and have working machines by Sunday evening.)

Then someone told me about @makerfaire, how awesome it is, and I decided to go. It was AMAZING to meet so many new people like me for the first time in my life - MAKERS 🤩 But now the fun part - a good half of the people I met and knew my printers thought Prusa was short for "Print USA." It is funny, amazing and if you think about it - it makes complete sense 🤔

On my way back home, I was thinking about it, that it is too funny to boringly and repeatedly explain that it is "just my family name." A couple of months later, a joke started circulating around Czechia, which loosely translates as "Everyone is a fool, only I am an airplane" 🤣 When I saw it, I immediately knew and started brainstorming ideas. With the final design being shown off at 2012 MakerFaire New York, as you can see in the picture below 😇

I don't take myself too seriously and like to do silly stuff like this t-shirt, but sometimes the joke ends up sticking around. It turned out, that the slogan is a great conversation starter. I had hundreds of lovely chats during my travels with random people on the street, airport or even hiking. Often resulting in people finding out about 3D printing for the first time and being excited about it 🧡

It is now more than a decade later, I think most people can't even imagine the "Print USA" scenario nowadays, and as Prusa matures as a brand, of course, I am thinking about the next "catchphrase", but I am keeping this silly one just a tiny bit longer 😉

Now that I think about it, the "Print USA" cases might soon increase in frequency again 😉🇺🇸

Happy printing 🧡💚
